item.title: Weez Gotti Sentenced To 41 Months In Federal Gun Case
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Weez Gotti received a 41-month federal sentence after pleading guilty to a gun charge that kept the North Richmond rapper jailed.
item.content:encoded:
North Richmond rapper Luis “Weez Gotti” Rincon has been sentenced to 41 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to a gun charge.

The Mercury News reported the sentence, bringing the latest chapter of his federal case to an end with three years and five months behind bars.

Weez Gotti, 30, was charged on April 22 with being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition under federal law. An official federal court record shows that a magistrate judge ordered him detained after a May 5 hearing.

The case began with a coordinated arrest at Weez Gotti’s North Richmond home. Crime Voice reported that U.S. Marshals and Contra Costa County sheriff’s deputies took him into custody on a federal warrant.

The outlet said officers recovered firearms and suspected drugs during the search and alleged that Weez Gotti tried to flee through a window before his arrest.

The May detention order focused on the firearm accusation and the rapper’s history.

The judge cited prior weapons convictions, evading police and violations of post-release community supervision. The order also said Weez Gotti was on parole when the charged conduct allegedly occurred and concluded that no release conditions would reasonably protect the community.

Before sentencing, federal prosecutors asked the judge to impose four years in prison.

He responded with a personal letter describing music as an outlet and reflecting on years spent in the criminal justice system. “The streets took everything from me, Your Honor,” he wrote.

The 41-month sentence came in seven months below the government’s request. It also followed Weez Gotti’s guilty plea to the firearm charge, resolving the central federal count without a trial.

item.title: Mathematics Recalls Contract Pushback & Questions Streaming Pay
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Mathematics recalled challenging standard contract terms and questioned streaming pay as his next Black Samson album approached.
item.content:encoded:
Mathematics recalled pushing back when a lawyer called contract terms standard, then questioned streaming compensation in a new interview about the business behind his music.

Speaking with The Hip Hop Museum, the Wu-Tang producer described a willingness to ask for more. “But I don’t want standard.” His reasoning: “The worst they can say is no.” He credited RZA, Divine and Power with teaching him about ownership.

That interview also addressed his dislike of streaming and desire for fair pay. He questioned who had set streaming’s pay guidelines.

He said physical purchases showed fans making an effort to support artists.

“But I’m in the record business, so you have to deal with streaming.” He advised artists to weigh their value realistically and know which terms they could accept or choose to walk away from.

Wu-Tang’s business history gives that conversation a longer frame. The group’s structure allowed members to make solo deals with different labels while staying in the collective, an arrangement described in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame’s official profile.

He also described how he makes records. In a 2025 AllHipHop interview with AllHipHop, Mathematics explained that his process for Black Samson: The Bastard Swordsman went beyond handing rappers a beat. He built out songs before bringing them to the artists.

He also said he appreciated when a rapper passed on a track that did not feel right. Getting a yes was not the only sign of respect in that process.

Mathematics wanted listeners to have time with a complete album, too. “I still believe in vision, in art you can hold,” he told AllHipHop.

His next project puts him back in that producer’s role. Black Samson: The Saga Continues is coming through DNA Music, with Mathematics producing the entire album. It follows the separate Black Samson: The Bastard Swordsman, released in April 2025.

“God Body,” the first single, paired Method Man and AZ. The forthcoming album’s guest list also includes Inspectah Deck, Masta Killa and U-God, bringing several Wu-Tang voices into a record built around Mathematics’ production. DNA Music has set November 6 for the release.

item.title: bbno$ Rallies Internet Stars For Palestinian Children’s Medical Relief
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: bbno$ will unite musicians and creators in Los Angeles on November 7 for a benefit supporting the Palestine Children's Relief Fund.
item.content:encoded:
bbno$ will bring internet stars to Los Angeles on Saturday, November 7, for a benefit whose proceeds will go to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund. The rapper’s “The Internet for Palestine” show will pair music and creator culture with aid for children.

bbno$ announced the concert after asking fellow artists in September to help put together a show for Palestine. His call followed his support for Macklemore after the Seattle rapper was removed from Ed Sheeran’s remaining U.S. tour dates.

“It’s the duty of an artist to use their voice to stand up for the oppressed,” bbno$ wrote on Instagram.

The initial lineup included MC Abdul, 6arelyHuman, Ellise, Joost, Mxmtoon, RomancePlanet, Ricky Montgomery, Scene Queen, Smosh and Sophie Powers. That mix gives the benefit a reach beyond rap, with online creators joining the musicians.

The benefit follows another major pledge from Macklemore. In September, he committed all $1 million of his net earnings from Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organizations helping Palestinians. PCRF was among those groups.

Macklemore also challenged New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft to match the donation. His own “Free Palestine Tour” ended October 30 at London’s OVO Arena Wembley. The venue pledged all concert proceeds to 12 organizations including PCRF.

All proceeds from bbno$’s benefit go to PCRF, which provides medical and humanitarian help to children in the Levant. The charity says it serves children “regardless of their nationality or religion.”

Its current Gaza relief and recovery campaign includes medical care, food, clean water and basic supplies. The work also extends to rebuilding health care and helping children cope with trauma.

PCRF’s recent surgical work gives some sense of the care its fundraising supports. The group said its Regional Surgical Program helped 357 children in September: 221 in the West Bank, 82 in Lebanon, 36 in Jordan and 18 in Egypt.

The charity also reported that 1,470 children received life-enhancing surgeries through the program during the first half of 2026.

The all-ages event is set for Shrine Expo Hall. Doors open at 5 P.M., with the show starting at 6 P.M., local time, according to the official event listing.

item.title: Isaiah Rashad Details Pressure To Represent Recovery And Queer Communities
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Isaiah Rashad discussed the pressure of representing recovery and queer communities in an interview about growth and forgiveness.
item.content:encoded:
Isaiah Rashad said the pressure to represent people in recovery and queer communities was too much for him to carry.

The TDE rapper from Chattanooga discussed those expectations with David Dennis Jr. in an Andscape interview, where they talked about sobriety, growth and forgiveness.

“But being the drug guy and the queer guy–it’s too much pressure. I’m just an imperfect person,” Rashad said.

His album It’s Been Awful explored childhood and generational trauma. It was also his first album since private footage of him was leaked in 2022.

Rashad had already discussed what came with being treated as a public example earlier this year.

In a separate May conversation with Dominic Fike, he talked about the expectations placed on him as a Black bisexual rapper and a person in recovery. He joked about not receiving the benefits he associated with Frank Ocean.

The two artists had also worked together: Fike appeared on “CAMERAS” on It’s Been Awful.

It’s Been Awful followed a five-year gap after 2021’s The House Is Burning. He addressed the limits of what he could offer listeners in an October interview with The Village Voice, too.

Rashad said messages about his music helping people were easier to receive than being told he had saved someone’s life.

“I’m not a counselor. I’m not giving advice to anybody. I’m answering the question because I have no advice,” he said.

The same interview described how he approached sobriety day to day. He said he stayed away from bars and kept a 12-step app on his phone.

Family was part of that account, too.

Rashad, who has three children, said being a parent pushed him to figure himself out.

His brother, Keem the Cipher, lived with him, traveled with him and served as the lead producer on It’s Been Awful. He also described his mother’s presence at important moments on the tour.

item.title: Janet Jackson’s Designer Says Super Bowl Reveal Was Planned
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Janet Jackson's longtime designer says the 2004 Super Bowl reveal was planned and wants Justin Timberlake to address the fallout.
item.content:encoded:
Janet Jackson’s longtime designer is reopening one of pop culture’s most disputed moments with a blunt claim: the 2004 Super Bowl costume reveal was not a wardrobe malfunction.

Wayne Scot Lukas told TMZ Live that the outfit worked as intended when Justin Timberlake tore away part of Jackson’s bustier during the halftime show.

Lukas said the costume concept had been changed shortly before the performance and that a planned reveal went far beyond what viewers were supposed to see.

“There was no wardrobe malfunction,” Lukas said. He also claimed Timberlake never apologized and that the backlash damaged his career.

The timing is not random. Timberlake is reportedly preparing a four-part Apple TV docuseries for December that will revisit the Super Bowl controversy.

Jackson is expected to discuss the incident in the series. Lukas said he was not asked to participate and wants Timberlake to use the project to tell the full story.

The historical record remains complicated. CBS maintained that the breast exposure was unscripted and unauthorized. Jackson said a costume reveal was added after the final rehearsal, but the full exposure was accidental.

Timberlake publicly apologized to Jackson and Britney Spears in 2021, acknowledging that he benefited from an entertainment system shaped by racism and misogyny.

The incident triggered more than 500,000 complaints to the Federal Communications Commission and a $550,000 fine against CBS stations.

A federal appeals court later threw out the penalty, finding that the FCC had changed its enforcement approach without adequate notice. The NFL’s archived account notes that nearly 90 million people watched the broadcast.

The exposure lasted less than a second, but the consequences stretched for years.

Broadcast delays changed, the legal fight reached federal court, and Jackson’s career paid a price that Timberlake’s did not. That imbalance is why each new account of the planning still attracts scrutiny more than two decades later.

item.title: Nelly, Gucci Mane & Rick Ross Join Morgan Wallen’s Sand In My Boots 2027
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Nelly, Gucci Mane and Rick Ross joined a rap-heavy Sand In My Boots 2027 bill, with passes set to go on sale November 6.
item.content:encoded:
Nelly, Gucci Mane and Rick Ross landed on Morgan Wallen’s 2027 Sand In My Boots lineup, giving Hip-Hop fans several reasons to watch a festival built around a country star.

Flo Rida, Juicy J, Project Pat and Ying Yang Twins also joined the bill announced November 2. The beach festival is set for May 21-23 in Gulf Shores, Alabama. Wallen, Kings of Leon and Ella Langley will headline.

Nelly already has a history of reaching country listeners. His 2021 album Heartland debuted at No. 7 on Billboard’s Top Country Albums chart. The project included “Lil Bit” with Florida Georgia Line, one of eight collaborations across its nine tracks.

Wallen said in the festival announcement, “I think it’s going to be really top-notch and we’re going to try to do it even better this time.”

The 2027 dates will mark the festival’s second edition. Sand In My Boots debuted in 2025, when Wallen shared headlining duties with Post Malone, Brooks & Dunn and HARDY. That first event sold out in two hours. There was no 2026 edition.

Wallen described the idea behind the festival when the first edition sold out: “We started talking about curating a festival that includes my friends, and artists who have influenced me, years ago.”

That mix is still part of the 2027 roster. Alongside the rap acts, the bill includes Kygo, Empire of the Sun and Girl Talk. Country performers include Cole Swindell, Midland, Koe Wetzel, Avery Anna and Kameron Marlowe.

Festival passes go on sale November 6 at 10 A.M. Central. Fans can register ahead of the sale to receive a code and purchase link. The site lists general admission at $676.87, including taxes and beach restoration fees, for the full weekend.

General admission includes beach club access and swimming. Party Pit passes are listed at $1,354.87 and include a front-of-stage viewing area at the main stage. VIP passes cost $2,484.87, while Super VIP is listed at $3,614.87.

The festival also offers hotel packages that bundle lodging with passes and shuttle transportation. Buyers can choose a payment plan with 25 percent down at checkout.

item.title: Rell Owns Past Mistakes As He Returns Directly To Fans
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: R&B artist Rell returned with "I'll Be There," a self-produced single he chose to sell straight to listeners through his own store.
item.content:encoded:
Rell explained why he left music for nearly a decade in a November 3 A&RFactory interview, describing setbacks and his mistakes.

The Southern California R&B singer, whose full name is Jarell Gaines, announced a November 4 return with “I’ll Be There.” He wrote, performed and produced the single himself and chose to sell it through his own online store.

“I got tired of losing,” he said. “I lost focus. I made poor decisions.”

He acknowledged damaging relationships and taking supporters for granted. He also described working at several churches almost six days a week while juggling production and live music. He had built several studios, including one in his family’s home, but said none became the space he had envisioned.

After stepping away from recording and performing, he worked as a behavioral technician, loaded warehouses and drove box trucks. His wife kept encouraging him to try music again. He recalled believing he was too old to come back.

“But my wife refused to let the dream die,” Rell said.

The interview also traced his work on “I’ll Be There”: he revised the verses and delivery while keeping the hook. He connected the song to accountability, relationships and his faith.

That wider meaning followed a change in the song’s direction. The release announcement described a track that began as a love ballad and grew into a reflection on being present for family and faith. According to the announcement, acoustic guitar and vocal harmonies sit alongside a Hip-Hop rhythm.

Based in California’s Inland Empire, Rell founded Jachord Studios. His official biography identifies creative ownership and artist development as parts of his work.

He said AI tools should treat human creators fairly, with particular concern for Black creators.

His return also offers a different way to reach listeners: the release plan sends buyers to his official store instead of traditional distribution platforms. The release announcement described plans to use Jachord Studios to build resources and collaboration opportunities for other independent artists.

The Payhip listing sets a $1.99 minimum, with buyers able to contribute more. The purchase provides a mastered MP3 for personal listening, with permanent access to the file. Buyers do not receive resale, sampling or commercial rights.

item.title: YouTube Expands AI Music Replacement With A YouTube-Only License
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: YouTube expanded its AI music replacement tool beyond the U.S., but the generated tracks come with a YouTube-only restriction.
item.content:encoded:
YouTube expanded its AI music replacement tool beyond the United States on November 3, giving more creators a way to swap out music hit with a copyright claim.

The replacement tracks come with a firm boundary: YouTube use only.

The company said the feature is now available in most countries outside the European Economic Area. Its announcement stated, “Music generated by this feature is intended solely for use in videos and other content that you create on YouTube.”

The generator offers four royalty-free instrumentals, each three minutes long. Creators can loop them, adjust the volume or download them. A download does not extend the license to other platforms.

The option sits inside YouTube Studio’s “Replace song” feature. Unlike tools built around a creator’s written prompt, this one does not accept custom text instructions. Creators can generate another set of choices if the first batch does not fit. They can preview the tracks and review their licensing information before using one.

YouTube’s help page says the claimed audio must be fully replaced before the claim is removed after processing. Other fixes remain available, including trimming the affected section, erasing the song or choosing music from the Audio Library.

The feature first reached U.S. desktop users earlier this year. Rene Ritchie introduced it on “Creator Insider” on May 1. The November update widened access, rather than marking the tool’s debut.

YouTube had planned a mobile version, but It said it was still unavailable in the Studio mobile app.

The kind of claim matters here.

Content ID can match music in an upload and let the rights owner block the video, track it or collect revenue from it. Those choices can vary by country. YouTube says monetization is the most common policy for music claims.

“Copyright claims are different from copyright removal requests and copyright strikes,” YouTube explains in its Content ID guidance. A Content ID claim usually affects the video rather than the channel. Replacing a track addresses the matching audio; it does not give the creator rights to the original song.

The expansion follows another AI music change on the platform. YouTube Music began rolling out AI song labels on October 14, with disclosure and detection rules covering generated beats and vocals.

Those rules distinguish generative AI from tools such as Auto-Tune and mastering. That system identifies how music was made. Studio’s replacement option serves a separate purpose: changing the music in an existing upload to resolve a claim.

Creators also have a lasting edit to weigh before saving. Since June 2025, changes saved through Studio’s editor cannot be undone with its old revert option.

item.title: Rapsody Says She Priced Her Shows At $25 & Took Loss To Set Up 2027
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Rapsody kept tickets near $25, sold out four cities and took a planned loss while laying groundwork for a bigger 2027 tour.
item.content:encoded:
Rapsody turned a four-city sold-out run into something bigger than a quick payday.

The North Carolina MC deliberately kept base tickets between $25 and $35 for October’s “This Broadcast Is Live Tour,” knowing the numbers would not add up in her favor.

According to Pollstar, the Oct. 16-23 run landed deeply in the red. VIP access stayed at $75, and the whole thing was treated more like a promotional investment than a conventional profit play.

Rapsody said the red ink was expected from the start. That loss came with a purpose.

“We didn’t make any money off this tour. I’m not going to tell you how much. But it’s worth it,” she said.

Rapsody said she wanted people to remember what happened in the room, feel part of a real community and leave as fans who would stick around after the final show. Cheap entry mattered because access was central to the idea, not a late marketing hook.

The public ticket listings back up the low-price strategy. Brooklyn tickets carried a $27.72 face value before a $7.27 fee, while a sold-out meet-and-greet upgrade showed demand for a closer experience. At Los Angeles’ Blue Note, bar admission was listed at $30 before $8.54 in fees, with table seating at $45 before a $10.54 fee.

This was also a test run for what comes next. Rapsody and her team are planning a more evolved, expanded 2027 tour tied to God Gotta Afro & Gold Hoops, with worldwide ambitions and the same focus on keeping the experience within reach.

No dates have been announced, so fans are getting a direction for the next chapter, not a finished itinerary.

The four-city route was first unveiled in September with stops built to bring the album into a live setting. At the time, Rapsody hinted that the concept could go “worldwide,” but kept the details open.

Now the strategy is clearer: use a small, affordable run to learn what works, deepen the bond with the audience and build toward a larger global outing.

“Our tour is a continuation of the storyline we created before I made the album. I’ve watched radio go from a lot of independently owned stations to a few owners, and now you’ve got playlisting, and DJs don’t have the freedom to play what they want to play. That’s the banning of a voice,” she tells me, assuredly. “Today you’ve got book bans, the dismantling of DEI, the rewriting and whitewashing of history. So we’re reversing the damage.”

The album at the center of that plan is Rapsody’s fifth.

In a KCLU/NPR interview, she discussed the spirituality and personal growth running through the project, including her questions about what God looks like and how those ideas connect to her own evolution.

Those themes gave the short tour more weight than a standard club run. It was built as an extension of the record and a way to let listeners experience that world together.

For an artist at Rapsody’s level, selling out and losing money sound like opposite outcomes. In this case, both facts were part of the design.

The four shows proved there was appetite for the album in a live room, while the ticket prices lowered the barrier for fans who might otherwise stay home.

Rapsody’s team is now carrying both lessons into its 2027 planning: demand exists, and access remains part of the brief.

item.title: Fans Furious After Daniel Caesar Cancels Seven Arena Shows For Health Reasons
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Daniel Caesar canceled seven Australia and Hawaii shows for health reasons, as ticket sellers provided refund instructions.
item.content:encoded:
Daniel Caesar canceled seven arena shows in Australia and Hawaii for health reasons. His first Australian arena tour had been due to start just days later.

“Unfortunately the Son of Spergy Australia and Hawaii shows are cancelled until further notice, due to health reasons,” Caesar wrote on Instagram Stories.

His statement did not name a health condition or offer new dates and fans were not happy.

“How disappointing you literally waited till the last second to cancel ur show I’m like very disappointed I’m not speaking for myself but I’m speaking for everyone that was looking forward to seeing you. If you gave further notice that would’ve been really appreciated but this is really disappointing getting our hopes up for nothing absolutely nothing,” one fans said.

The Australian run included Sydney’s Afterpay Arena on November 5 and 6. Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena had shows set for November 8 and 9. Brisbane Entertainment Centre was due to host him on November 12.

Two Honolulu concerts at Neal S. Blaisdell Arena on November 14 and 15 were also canceled.

The run had been announced in August. Caesar last toured Australia in 2023, playing venues including the Sydney Opera House Forecourt and Melbourne’s Sidney Myer Music Bowl. The dates were part of the tour behind his fourth album, Son of Spergy, released in October 2025.

Caesar had also withdrawn from Johns Hopkins University’s Hoptoberfest, where Cardi B stepped in as headliner. That withdrawal was attributed to unforeseen circumstances.

The university show was moved from October 31 to November 1, when Cardi performed. Caesar announced the booking on October 19 and tickets sold out on October 21, with hundreds of students joining the waitlist. Existing tickets remained valid for the replacement show.

The Ticketek notice for Sydney told buyers how they would get their money back. “All tickets purchased (including refundable ticket purchases, if relevant) will be automatically refunded in full to the original payment method used,” the notice said.

Ticketek said most refunds should take five business days, though some could take up to 20. Customers who paid through an agency or with a gift voucher must provide bank details through Ticketek’s official page by November 17.

In Hawaii, Ticketmaster listed both Honolulu dates as canceled. Its November 15 event notice said it would process refunds after receiving funds from the organizer, with a 14-to-21-day window. “If the tickets were transferred to you, the refund will go to the fan who originally purchased the tickets from Ticketmaster,” Ticketmaster added.

“This trash did the same thing 3 years ago how shameful you are,” one angry commenter fumed. Another wrote: “Don’t do this to me man, I’ll pay the emergency bills 💔💔.”
